prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: Prototype Controller Board BOM (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 8 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 17px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Part number" · longest unbreakable word 184px · one-line width 184px
  col 2: header "Description" · longest unbreakable word 119px · one-line width 584px
  col 3: header "Qty" · longest unbreakable word 29px · one-line width 29px
  col 4: header "Unit price" · longest unbreakable word 65px · one-line width 78px
  col 5: header "Supplier" · longest unbreakable word 148px · one-line width 148px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 752px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 751px.
Fixed: content, font, 17px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Your understanding so far: {"purpose":"Specify the components needed to build a prototype controller board, including quantities, prices and sources.","reading":"Readers identify each part, check its specifications, then scan quantity, unit price and supplier for purchasing. Each row should remain easy to follow across the table.","groups":["Part number and Description identify and characterize each component.","Qty and Unit price are compact purchasing figures that readers may compare down their columns.","Supplier completes the purchasing information for each part."],"keep_intact":["Part numbers and supplier names should remain intact where possible, because breaks make exact identification and sourcing harder.","Quantities, individual prices and technical values should remain intact.","Keep the Unit price header on one line where space permits."],"may_wrap":["Descriptions can wrap naturally at spaces and punctuation; longer descriptions will create row height that can absorb wrapping in other cells.","The Unit price header can wrap if that space is more valuable to descriptions.","If necessary, long part numbers or supplier names may break, with a cost to scanning and exact identification."]}

The first image is the one-line content overview. The other images are real browser renders of your current designs:
Design r0A: widths [205, 241, 50, 86, 169] · table 752×606px · row heights [66, 66, 66, 92, 92, 66, 66, 92] · column headers wrapped 1/5 · tallest cell 3 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r0B: widths [175, 286, 50, 86, 154] · table 752×553px · row heights [66, 66, 66, 92, 66, 66, 66, 66] · column headers wrapped 1/5 · tallest cell 3 lines · mid-word splits 4
Design r0C: widths [205, 226, 50, 101, 169] · table 752×632px · row heights [39, 66, 66, 118, 92, 66, 92, 92] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 4 lines · mid-word splits 0

Look carefully at each render as a whole and in detail. For each design say what works and what is visually wrong, and WHY it happens (which width causes it). Then propose up to 3 improved designs: refine the most promising, fix the problems you saw, and try a new idea if an important alternative is unexplored. If no design can be meaningfully improved, set "done": true and return no new designs.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"critique":[{"design":"name","good":"","problems":"","cause":""}],"done":false,"designs":[{"name":"short-name","widths":[int px],"change":"what you changed and why"}]}
